pharm: Provides bicarbonate to buffer hydrogen ion, raise blood and urine pH, and correct metabolic acidosis; also acts as an antacid and urinary alkalinizer.
quick: Cardiac arrest: 1 mEq/kg IV; metabolic acidosis: 2-5 mEq/kg over 4-8 h
Oral antacid: take 1-3 h after meals
Use if clearly needed; generally low risk
Caution; sodium retention, fluid overload, alkalosis
Arterial pH/blood gases, electrolytes, plasma CO2, fluid status
summary: Sodium bicarbonate is a systemic alkalinizer used IV to treat metabolic acidosis (severe renal disease, uncontrolled diabetes, shock/dehydration, cardiac arrest, severe lactic acidosis), to alkalinize urine in certain poisonings (salicylates, methanol) and hemolytic reactions, and to manage severe bicarbonate-losing diarrhea. The 8.4% injection is hypertonic. Orally it is an antacid and urinary alkalinizer. Overly aggressive therapy causes metabolic alkalosis, hypernatremia, and fluid overload; it is contraindicated when chloride is being lost (vomiting/GI suction) or with diuretics causing hypochloremic alkalosis. Extravasation of the IV solution can cause tissue necrosis.
indications: Treatment of metabolic acidosis (severe renal disease, uncontrolled diabetes, circulatory insufficiency from shock or severe dehydration, extracorporeal circulation, cardiac arrest, severe primary lactic acidosis)
Certain drug intoxications - barbiturates (dissociation of barbiturate-protein complex), salicylate or methyl alcohol poisoning
Hemolytic reactions requiring urinary alkalinization to reduce nephrotoxicity of hemoglobin breakdown products
Severe diarrhea with significant bicarbonate loss
Oral: antacid for dyspepsia/hyperacidity and urinary alkalinization (separate formulations)

dosage.d: 44.6-100 mEq (one to two 50 mL vials of 8.4%) initially, ~1 mEq/kg
dosage.t: Then 50 mL (44.6-50 mEq) every 5-10 min if needed
dosage.n: Guided by arterial pH and blood gases; not routine in all arrests
Dose depends on severity (degree of CO2/pH lowering and clinical state); titrate stepwise
Monitor blood gases, plasma osmolarity, arterial lactate, hemodynamics, and cardiac rhythm
Replace potassium as needed; monitor urine pH

dosage.t: Up to 4 times daily, 1-3 h after meals and at bedtime
dosage.n: Short-term use; high sodium load (separate oral labeling)

admin: Administer the 8.4% injection intravenously; it is hypertonic - infuse with care to avoid rapid rises in plasma sodium
Plan bicarbonate therapy stepwise; response to a given dose is not precisely predictable
Avoid extravasation - the alkaline solution can cause chemical cellulitis with tissue necrosis/sloughing
Do not mix with calcium-containing solutions or with norepinephrine/dobutamine (incompatible/precipitation)
Do not use if the solution contains a precipitate; use aseptic technique for additives
In cardiac arrest, give as rapid IV dose; otherwise prefer slower infusion to limit hypernatremia
moa: Provides bicarbonate (HCO3-) that buffers excess hydrogen ion, raising blood pH and reversing acidosis; sodium (Na+) supports extracellular fluid/electrolyte balance. In urine, increased bicarbonate raises urinary pH, enhancing renal excretion of weak acids (e.g., salicylates) and reducing precipitation of hemoglobin/myoglobin breakdown products. As an antacid it neutralizes gastric acid.

absolute: Loss of chloride from vomiting or continuous GI suction
Patients receiving diuretics that produce hypochloremic alkalosis

preg: No human teratogenicity data provided in the injection label; used when clearly needed to correct maternal acidosis. Generally considered low risk when used appropriately.
lact: Considered compatible with breastfeeding when used appropriately for maternal indications.
renal: Use with great care, if at all, in severe renal insufficiency - sodium retention, fluid overload, and metabolic alkalosis can result. Monitor electrolytes, fluid status, and acid-base balance closely.
hepatic: Use with caution in cirrhosis or other conditions with edema and sodium retention, as the sodium load may worsen fluid accumulation.

major: Calcium-containing IV solutions (precipitation - do not co-infuse)
Norepinephrine and dobutamine (inactivated/incompatible in the same line)
moderate: Drugs whose renal elimination is pH-dependent - alkalinization increases excretion of acidic drugs (salicylates, barbiturates, methotrexate) and decreases excretion of basic drugs (amphetamines, quinidine)
minor: Oral antacid form reduces absorption of some drugs (e.g., iron, tetracyclines, certain antibiotics) - separate dosing
interactions.food: Oral antacid: take 1-3 hours after meals.
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor arterial pH/blood gases, plasma CO2, serum electrolytes, and urine pH (for alkalinization targets).

common: Metabolic alkalosis (muscle twitching, irritability, tetany) with overuse
serious: Chemical cellulitis with tissue necrosis on extravasation
Cerebral acidosis/paradoxical CNS effects with rapid correction
rare: Intracranial hemorrhage (neonates with rapid hypertonic infusion)
Milk-alkali syndrome (chronic oral use with calcium)
emergency: Severe alkalosis with tetany or seizures

monitoring: Serum sodium, potassium, calcium, chloride, and bicarbonate
Plasma osmolarity and (in acidosis with shock) arterial lactate, hemodynamics, cardiac rhythm
Fluid balance and signs of overload/edema
Urine pH when used for urinary alkalinization
counsel: This is given in hospital to correct acid in your blood or to make your urine less acidic; the team will check blood tests frequently
Tell staff immediately of pain, swelling, or burning at the IV site
If you use oral baking-soda antacid at home, take it 1-3 hours after meals and not long-term without advice
People with heart, kidney, or blood-pressure problems should use it cautiously because of its sodium content
Report muscle twitching, cramps, or tingling
pk: Regulated by renal handling; not a fixed value
Depends on dose, acid-base state, and renal compensation
20-25 C; avoid excessive heat; protect from freezing
pearls: The 8.4% injection is hypertonic (1 mEq/mL each Na+ and HCO3-); 84 mg = 1 mEq
Plan bicarbonate stepwise and recheck blood gases - over-correction causes alkalosis, hypokalemia, and hypocalcemic tetany
Do not co-infuse with calcium (precipitation) or with catecholamines like norepinephrine/dobutamine (inactivation)
Routine use in cardiac arrest is no longer recommended; reserve for hyperkalemia, severe acidosis, or specific toxins (e.g., TCA overdose)
Urinary alkalinization is key for salicylate and methanol poisoning and to protect kidneys in pigment (hemoglobin/myoglobin) nephropathy
Extravasation causes alkaline tissue necrosis - treat with elevation, warmth, and local lidocaine/hyaluronidase
missed: Administered and titrated by clinicians during acute care; dosing is guided by blood gases rather than a fixed schedule, so there is no patient-managed missed dose. For oral antacid use, take when symptoms occur as directed.
overdose: Overdose produces metabolic alkalosis (hyperirritability, tetany), hypernatremia, and fluid overload. Stop the bicarbonate; manage according to severity - give 0.9% sodium chloride IV, potassium chloride for hypokalemia, and calcium gluconate for tetany; ammonium chloride or an acidifying agent may be needed for severe alkalosis.
